# Article A pro-carcinogenic bacterial toxin binds claudin-4 to cleave E-cadherin

Maxwell T. White1,11, Kang Wang2,3,4,11, Hailong Zhang5,6,9, Ulrich Eckhard7, Karthik Hullahalli5,6,10, Jason Chen1, Shaoguang Wu1, Abby L. Geis1, Jie Zhang2,3,4, Jessica Queen1, F. Xavier Gomis-Ruth7,12, Matthew K. Waldor5,6,12, Min Dong2,3,4,12 ✉ & Cynthia L. Sears1,8,12 ✉

The human colon is colonized by trillions of bacteria that play substantial roles in human health and disease1. Epidemiological and experimental studies suggest that certain colonic bacteria can stimulate the development and progression of colorectal cancer2. One such bacterium, enterotoxigenic Bacteroides fragilis, drives colon tumour formation through the action of a single toxin, the B. fragilis toxin (BFT)3,4. BFT is a metalloprotease that binds to a colonic epithelial cell receptor and causes cleavage of the E-cadherin ectodomain, leading to epithelial barrier disruption, inflammation and increased cellular proliferation4–6. However, the identity of the BFT receptor is unknown and the molecular mechanism of BFT-initiated E-cadherin cleavage is not well understood. Here we identify claudin-4 as a BFT receptor through a genome-wide CRISPR screen and demonstrate that claudin-4 binding promotes BFT-mediated cleavage of cell surface E-cadherin. Our work both sheds light on BFT’s mechanism of action and opens avenues for the development of anti-BFT therapies, which may prove useful for colorectal cancer prevention and treatment of acute enterotoxigenic B. fragilis infection.

Recent evidence suggests that certain members of the human gut microbiota promote the development of colorectal cancer2. Toxigenic strains of Bacteroides fragilis, a ubiquitous colonic bacterium, are epidemiologically associated with colorectal neoplasia in humans7–9 and drive colon tumorigenesis in susceptible mice3,4. Colon tumorigenesis induced by these enterotoxigenic B. fragilis (ETBF) is dependent on a single approximately 21-kDa metalloprotease, the B. fragilis toxin (BFT; also known as fragilysin), which disrupts the colonic epithelial barrier and triggers a pro-carcinogenic mucosal TH17 immune response4. Despite its potent ability to induce colon inflammation and tumorigenesis3,6, as well as to contribute to diarrhoeal disease10 and lethal B. fragilis sepsis11, the molecular mechanism of BFT is not well understood. BFT toxicity on colonic epithelial cells is characterized by toxin binding to an unknown cell surface receptor12 and rapid cleavage of the E-cadherin ectodomain5,6, followed by nuclear β-catenin translocation, cell rounding and stimulation of cellular proliferation4,5. Rather than resembling other bacterial metalloproteases, BFT shows striking structural homology to mammalian a-disintegrin-and-metalloproteinase enzymes (ADAMs)13,14, which cleave cell surface proteins, including E-cadherin, to regulate various physiological and pathophysiological processes15. This suggests that BFT may be derived from an adamalysin/ADAM xenolog after horizontal gene transfer to B. fragilis from a mammalian intestinal host cell13. However, although ADAMs

cleave E-cadherin directly, releasing an approximately 80-kDa soluble fragment from the cell surface similar to the fragment produced by BFT15,16, previous studies have failed to demonstrate direct E-cadherin cleavage by BFT in biochemical assays5,17. These reports, combined with the observation of toxin-receptor binding12, have given rise to multiple incomplete models of BFT’s action implicating host cell signalling and proteases in E-cadherin cleavage10,12,16, which lack key evidence. As ETBF can be detected in up to 20% of healthy individuals18,19 and is strongly implicated in colorectal neoplasia3,4,7,8, a more detailed understanding of the initial molecular events in BFT toxicity is paramount to the development of strategies to prevent and treat ETBF-associated diseases. Herein, we identify the tight junction protein claudin-4 as a BFT receptor and show that claudin-4 binding promotes BFT-mediated cleavage of the E-cadherin ectodomain. Our results provide evidence of a previously undescribed mechanism for the modulation of microbial protease activity through host cell receptor binding. This pathway may be important in general for targeting of proteolytic activity to key cell types and targets of interest in the complex environment of the gut microbiome. Furthermore, our findings hold direct relevance to the development of BFT inhibitors, as blocking claudin-4 binding could mitigate BFT toxicity without affecting closely related mammalian metalloproteases.

## CRISPR screen for BFT host factors

As the molecular events in BFT toxicity precedent to E-cadherin cleavage were unknown, except for demonstration of binding to an unidentified receptor12, we initiated a genome-wide CRISPR-knockout (KO) screen for host determinants of BFT toxicity. Previous screens of this type relied on cell survival as the mechanism to select toxin-resistant cell populations20, but BFT does not kill cells. As BFT treatment results in release of the E-cadherin ectodomain from the cell surface, we instead decided to use surface E-cadherin staining to select BFT-resistant cell populations, with the rationale that BFT-resistant cells should retain their surface E-cadherin following BFT treatment. We chose the colon carcinoma cell line HT29 for the screen because it is the most established cell line used to study BFT11,12,14 and is tractable in genome-wide CRISPR screens21. Briefly, two independent replicates of the Avana CRISPR-KO library in Cas9-expressing HT29 cells21 (libraries A and B) were treated with recombinant His6-tagged BFT (Extended Data Fig. 1a), dissociated into single-cell suspensions, stained with

an antibody against the E-cadherin ectodomain and sorted to yield the top 10% of cells retaining surface E-cadherin (Fig. 1a). Collected cells were expanded and subjected to an identical second round of selection to further enrich for BFT-resistant cell populations. The DNA sequences encoding the guide RNAs (gRNAs) in the input and selected cell populations were PCR amplified and read out by next-generation sequencing. Gene-level enrichment values and statistical significance scores were calculated using MAGeCK22, and hits were defined as significantly enriched genes after the second round of selection in both screen replicates at false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05 (Fig. 1b, Extended Data Fig. 2 and Supplementary Tables 1–4). The tight junction protein claudin-4 stood out as the clear top hit (Fig. 1b) with its closest paralogue claudin-3 ranking fourth in mean fold change23 (Extended Data Fig. 2b). We noted that the hits largely did not cluster into obvious biological pathways, the exception being PIGU and PIGL, genes involved in the synthesis and attachment of the glyco­- sylphosphatidylinositol anchor to glycosylphosphatidylinositolanchored proteins24. ## Claudin-4 is critical for BFT toxicity

Given the enrichment of claudins-4 and -3 in our screen, and their known ability to serve as receptors for the pore-forming toxin, Clostridium perfringens enterotoxin (CPE)29,30, we sought to validate the role of these claudins in BFT toxicity. We began by constructing claudin-4-knockout (C4-KO) and claudin-3-knockout (C3-KO) HT29 cell lines using CRISPR– Cas9. Disruption of the targeted open reading frames was confirmed by Sanger sequencing and loss of the encoded proteins was confirmed

by immunoblot (Extended Data Fig. 3a,b). HT29 cells are exquisitely BFT-sensitive, resulting in cell rounding at picomolar toxin concen­ trations27. C4-KO, but unexpectedly not C3-KO, HT29-Cas9 cells showed resistance to cell rounding induced by BFT (0.8 ng ml−1, 37 pM) (Fig. 2a). To quantify the magnitude of BFT resistance of the knockout cell lines, we measured the surface E-cadherin levels of wild-type (WT), C4-KO and C3-KO HT29-Cas9 cells by flow cytometry after treatment with varying BFT concentrations. C4-KO, but not C3-KO, HT29-Cas9 cells showed 20-fold resistance to BFT-mediated E-cadherin cleavage compared with WT cells (Fig. 2b,c). The BFT sensitivity of C4-KO HT29-Cas9 cells was restored by expression of GFP-tagged claudin-4 (Fig. 2a–c). Strikingly, monoclonal claudin-4/claudin-3 double-knockout (C4/C3-KO) HT29 cell lines showed an average of around 500-fold BFT resistance (Fig. 2d,e), indicating that claudin-3 can partially compensate for the absence of claudin-4 in BFT toxicity. To test the generalizability of these findings, we generated C4-KO and C3-KO T84 cells, which can be cultured as polarized monolayers that recapitulate structural features of the colonic epithelium, including tight junctions31. The catalytically inactive mutant BFT(E349Q) did not decrease monolayer TER, indicating that catalytic activity is required for sustained epithelial barrier disruption (Extended Data Fig. 4a). Depletion of monolayer claudin-4, but not claudin-3, also conferred resistance to basolateral BFT (Extended Data Fig. 4b–d). Consistent with results in HT29 cells, double-knockout of claudins-4 and -3 resulted in even further BFT resistance (Fig. 2g), despite impairing barrier function at baseline (Fig. 2f). Therefore, claudin-4 is critical to BFT toxicity in colonic epithelial cell culture models and claudin-3 can partially compensate for this function in the absence of claudin-4. Given that claudin-4 and claudin-3 are the two most closely related human claudins23 (Extended Data Fig. 3c), the lack of an altered phenotype in C3-KO single-knockout cell lines prompted an investigation of potential off-target activity in the Avana library gRNAs targeting CLDN3 (ref. 34). Indeed, three of four gRNAs in the Avana library targeting CLDN3 harboured only one or two mismatches against the corresponding CLDN4 sequence (Extended Data Fig. 2c). The Cutting Frequency Determination off-target scores34 of the Avana CLDN3 gRNAs against the corresponding CLDN4 sequences correlated with their enrichment in both screen replicates, whereas their CRISPRater on-target scores did not35 (Extended Data Fig. 2d). Thus, it is likely that off-target activity against CLDN4 drove the enrichment of CLDN3 in our screens.

## Claudin-4 is a BFT receptor

To test the hypothesis that claudin-4 is a BFT receptor, we measured BFT binding to the surface of WT, C4-KO and C3-KO HT29 cells using an anti-His6 antibody to stain recombinant His6-tagged BFT. Although WT and C3-KO HT29 cells demonstrated stable BFT binding to the cell surface evidenced by robust surface anti-His6 staining following BFT treatment, C4-KO cells showed a total absence of stable surface BFT binding (Fig. 3a). This result was further validated by immunoblot for cell surface-bound BFT (Fig. 3b). Expression of GFP-claudin-4 (GFP-C4) in C4-KO HT29 cells resulted in a lower claudin-4 protein level compared with WT cells, with some apparent hydrolysis of the linker region to yield untagged claudin-4, but restored BFT binding proportionally to claudin-4 expression (Fig. 3b). BFT co-immunoprecipitated with claudin-4, but not claudin-2, in BFT-treated HT29 cells, indicating a physical interaction between BFT and claudin-4 (Fig. 3c). Furthermore, expression of GFP-tagged claudin-4, but not claudin-2 or claudin−3, in 293T cells conferred the ability to stably bind BFT (Fig. 3d). Pulldown assays showed direct binding of untagged BFT (Extended Data Fig. 1b) to a His6-tagged soluble claudin-4 analogue displaying native extracellular segments (ECSs) (CLN4_20 from ref. 36, herein referred to as CLN4sol), but not when its ECSs were swapped with those of claudin-2 to form C4sol(C2-ECS) (Extended Data Fig. 5a,b and Fig. 3e). Analytical size exclusion chromatography (SEC) and SEC coupled with multi-angle light scattering (SEC-MALS) demonstrated that CLN4sol forms large oligomers in solution as previously described36. ## Claudin-4 enables surface BFT activity

As no host cell proteases were identified in our CRISPR screen, we hypothesized that binding to claudin-4 may facilitate direct cleavage of surface-localized E-cadherin by BFT. We made use of 293T cells, which do not express claudins37 or plasma membrane-localized E-cadherin38, as a reductionist background system to determine whether claudin-4 binding enables BFT to cleave E-cadherin at the cell surface. First, 293T cells were transfected with mCherry-tagged human E-cadherin

(Ecad-mCherry) and treated with BFT, and surface E-cadherin levels were measured by flow cytometry. Although exposure to even high BFT concentrations (100 ng ml−1, 4.6 nM) did not induce any detectable cleavage of surface Ecad-mCherry alone, co-expression of GFP-C4 enabled robust BFT-mediated Ecad-mCherry cleavage evidenced by loss of surface E-cadherin staining (Fig. 4a). GFP-claudin-3 (GFP-C3) also enabled Ecad-mCherry cleavage, although to a lesser extent than GFP-C4, whereas GFP-claudin-2 did not support any detectable cleavage (Fig. 4b). The observation that claudin-3 expression enabled low-level BFT activity, along with its knockout showing an altered phenotype only on a claudin-4 knockout background, supports the conclusion that claudin-3 may be a further lower-affinity BFT receptor. ## Claudin-4 mutational analysis

We next sought to identify the key regions of claudin-4 involved in BFT binding and E-cadherin cleavage. Claudins consist of a minimal cytoplasmic N-terminus followed by four transmembrane segments connected by two ECSs, ECS1 and ECS2, and a cytoplasmic C-terminal domain (CTD)23. Residues in ECS1 and ECS2 are involved in claudin– claudin interactions23 and CPE binding29, whereas the CTD mediates interactions with intracellular binding partners such as ZO-1 (ref. 40) and Src-family kinases41. To determine whether CTD-mediated interactions with intercellular proteins are required for BFT-mediated E-cadherin cleavage, we generated a claudin-4 CTD deletion mutant, C4(ΔCTD) (Fig. 4c). GFP-C4(ΔCTD) enabled cleavage of E-cadherin to nearly the same extent as WT GFP-C4 (Fig. 4d), indicating that BFT activity does not require the claudin CTD involved in tight junction localization40 and signalling41. The modestly reduced expression level and BFT binding of the ΔCTD mutant suggests that the CTD may indirectly affect BFT binding and activity through effects on claudin stability or localization (Extended Data Fig. 6a). Next, we interrogated the roles of ECS1 and ECS2 by generating chimeric claudin-4 mutants C4(ECS13) and C4(ECS23) in which either the ECS1 or ECS2 sequence of claudin-4 was replaced by the corresponding claudin-3 sequence (Fig. 4c and Extended Data Fig. 6b). Although both GFP-C4(ECS13) and GFP-C4(ECS23) exhibited reduced BFT binding and E-cadherin cleavage compared with WT GFP-C4, the impairment of GFP-C4(ECS13) was more severe and phenocopied GFP-C3 (Fig. 4d,e and Extended Data Fig. 6a). Given that the ECS1 sequence of claudin-4 harbours only three amino acid differences from claudin-3 (T33S, V41I and T45N) (Extended Data Fig. 6b), we created and tested each individual claudin-4 to claudin-3 point mutant in our BFT binding and E-cadherin cleavage assays. Remarkably, the single substitution T45N within ECS1 completely abrogated stable BFT binding and reduced BFT-mediated E-cadherin cleavage to the level supported by GFP-C3 (Fig. 4d,e and Extended Data Fig. 6a). Surface biotinylation showed reduced extracellular accessibility of 293T cell-expressed GFP-C4(ECS23) compared with the WT protein, possibly owing to steric hinderance resulting from claudin polymerization induced by the claudin-3 ECS2 sequence42, whereas the other mutants were biotinylated similarly to WT GFP-C4 (Extended Data Fig. 6d,e). Overall, these data support involvement of both ECS1 and ECS2 sequences in BFT binding and E-cadherin cleavage, with residue T45 within ECS1 playing a particularly critical role. The effect of the ECS2 sequence may be dependent on modulation of claudin accessibility.

## Model of cell surface BFT proteolysis

The simplest model consistent with our data is that claudin binding facilitates direct cleavage of cell surface E-cadherin by BFT. To gain insight into how claudin-4 binding may promote BFT-mediated E-cadherin cleavage, we modelled the claudin-4:BFT:E-cadherin ternary complex using AlphaFold 3 (AF3)43 (Extended Data Fig. 7). The AF3-predicted structural model showed BFT contacting both claudin-4 extracellular sequences and poised to cleave E-cadherin in the linker region between its extracellular domain 5 and transmembrane helix, with the transmembrane helices of claudin-4 and E-cadherin aligned as if positioned in the same plasma membrane (Extended Data Fig. 7a–c). E-cadherin residues Lys697–Val701 were threaded through the BFT active site, closely matching the experimentally determined ADAM10 cleavage site after Pro700 (ref. 15) (Extended Data Fig. 7d). We verified

that BFT could cleave the E-cadherin sequence Lys697–Ala703 using a fluorogenic peptide substrate (Extended Data Fig. 7e,f). The positioning of E-cadherin, BFT and claudin-4 in the model relative to the plasma membrane boundary suggests that BFT is recruited to the membrane surface by claudin-4 binding (Extended Data Fig. 7d). Thus, we hypothesized that BFT relies on claudin-4 binding to access the sterically hindered E-cadherin cleavage site close to the membrane, similar to the recently elucidated mechanism of ADAM10 active site positioning by tetraspanin 15 binding44. To test this model, we generated Ecad-mCherry mutants containing varied mutations in the membrane-proximal linker region (Extended Data Fig. 8a). Mutating the putative BFT cleavage site residues Pro-Val to Gly-Gly significantly reduced BFT-mediated cleavage in the presence of GFP-C4 (Extended Data Fig. 8b). Shifting the cleavage site closer to the membrane by deleting four membrane-proximal amino acids reduced cleavage significantly more than deleting four amino acids distal to the cleavage site, whereas shifting the cleavage site further from the membrane by inserting a ten-amino-acid flexible linker reduced cleavage by the same amount (Extended Data Fig. 8b). Notably, no tested mutation completely ablated cleavage, suggesting that although BFT has a potentially broad substrate specificity45, toxin recruitment to its native E-cadherin cleavage sequence contributes to optimal proteolysis. The AF3-predicted model has substantial limitations. The claudin-4 ECSs interacting with BFT were generally modelled with low confidence (Extended Data Fig. 7b), precluding interpretation of the molecular details of BFT:claudin-4 binding. Furthermore, the AF3 model did not explain the role of claudin-4 residue T45 in BFT binding as its sidechain pointed away from the predicted BFT binding site, consistent with the crystal structure of claudin-4 bound to the C-terminal fragment of CPE30 (Extended Data Fig. 8c). It is intriguing to hypothesize that residue T45 may interact with a cell surface co-receptor, similar to the critical claudin-1 residue I32 in hepatitis C viral entry, which modulates interaction with co-receptor CD81 (refs. 46,47). Alternatively, the T45N substitution may shift claudin-4 to a conformation less permissive to BFT binding. Future structural and biochemical studies are needed to fully elucidate and validate the mechanism of BFT-mediated E-cadherin cleavage at the cell surface.

## Soluble claudin-4 analogue blocks BFT

Previous studies have demonstrated blockage of CPE toxicity using a soluble claudin-4 peptide29. Given the cleavage site recruitment mechanism suggested by the AF model, we wondered whether CLN4sol could block BFT toxicity by competitively blocking its binding to claudins on the colonic epithelium. Indeed CLN4sol, but not C4sol(C2-ECS), blocked BFT-mediated E-cadherin degradation in HT29 cells (Extended Data Fig. 8d). To test the hypothesis that claudin-4-based therapy could mitigate BFT-mediated disease in vivo, we utilized a model in which BFT is injected directly into the caecum of mice (Fig. 5a). Caecal injection of BFT resulted in extensive colonic epithelial cell shedding and oedema visualized by histological staining (Fig. 5b). Co-injection of CLN4sol, but not C4sol(C2-ECS), significantly reduced BFT-mediated epithelial cell shedding and oedema (Fig. 5c,d). Furthermore, mice injected with C4sol(C2-ECS) and BFT displayed extensive loss of cell membrane E-cadherin staining, whereas mice injected with CLN4sol and BFT retained largely intact E-cadherin (Fig. 5e). Injection with CLN4sol or C4sol(C2-ECS) alone did not affect caecal architecture or E-cadherin staining (Extended Data Fig. 9). Together, these results show that blocking the interaction between BFT and claudin-4 has the potential to prevent ETBF-mediated damage to colonic tissues.

Although claudin-4 is a known receptor for CPE, a pore-forming toxin, BFT uses claudin-4 binding for a distinct biochemical purpose—cleavage of a membrane-proximal protein substrate. We hypothesize that claudin-4 binding recruits BFT to the surface of the plasma membrane, allowing it to access the E-cadherin cleavage site. Although fractions of cellular claudin-4 and E-cadherin are localized to tight and adherens junctions, respectively, substantial pools of both are mobile on the membrane48,49. As BFT binds diffusely to the plasma membrane12, rather than in a pattern localized to the tight junction, we favour a model in which BFT bound to non-junctional claudin-4 encounters and cleaves E-cadherin by lateral diffusion (Extended Data Fig. 10). Many questions related to BFT’s mechanism of action remain. Most prominently, further studies are needed to understand how apical BFT bypasses tight junctions to gain access to E-cadherin at the basolateral membrane. A tempting explanation is that BFT first

targets sites of local tight junction derangement, such as the cell extrusion sites used by Listeria monocytogenes to access E-cadherin from the apical surface50,51. BFT-mediated cleavage of apically accessible E-cadherin at these sites could impair epithelial repair after cell extrusion, leaving holes for further BFT molecules to pass through. Another possibility is that BFT directly disrupts apical tight junctions through claudin binding. In this scenario, one would expect some degree of T84 monolayer TER disruption with apical BFT(E349Q), which we did not observe (Extended Data Fig. 4a), although we cannot rule out the possibility of transient disruption undetected by our assay. Following lamina propria niche acquisition by ETBF52, basolateral claudins and E-cadherin would be directly accessible by BFT. Whether junctional or non-junctional E-cadherin molecules are preferentially cleaved by BFT is also an open question. Finally, we cannot rule out the possibility that other host cell mole­ cules serve as further BFT receptors or co-receptors, as our CRISPR- KO screening strategy is intrinsically unable to provide information about essential genes. A co-receptor that increases the affinity of BFT:claudin-4 binding would help to explain the critical role of residue T45 in claudin-4 BFT binding and E-cadherin cleavage, as discussed above. Given the partial redundancy of claudins-4 and -3 in BFT toxicity (Figs. 2 and 4), other claudins expressed in human colon tissue, such as claudin-1, -3, -5, -6 and -7 (ref. 55), are potential candidates for secondary BFT receptors. In the future, CRISPRi56 and proximity labelling57 approaches may be considered to explore the full space of potential BFT receptors, co-receptors and cell surface modulators. Whereas other bacterial proteases cleave epithelial cell surface proteins such as E-cadherin, BFT displays a distinct mechanism in which its activity is modulated by binding to a host cell receptor. This mechanism potentially benefits ETBF by conveying exquisite specificity for target cells and allowing BFT to be active at low concentrations in the highly complex microbial community of the colon. Similar to the structure of BFT itself, this mechanism is reminiscent of the mammalian plasma membrane-tethered sheddase ADAM10, which is poised to cleave specific substrates, such as N-cadherin and Notch, through interactions with distinct tetraspanin proteins44,58. Notably, BFT activates Notch signalling in breast cancer cells59, indicating that BFT, similar to ADAM10, may cleave other cell surface proteins that play yet-undiscovered roles in toxicity and tumorigenesis. Our work further posits blocking claudin binding as a strategy to mitigate the deleterious effects of BFT, a topic of recent interest2,14,52. As metalloprotease inhibitor drugs are hindered by musculoskeletal toxicities stemming from off-target activity60, specific targeting of claudin binding represents an attractive alternative for anti-BFT therapy in ETBF-mediated diarrhoeal disease10, sepsis11 and colorectal neoplasia3,4,7,8.

Screening CRISPR-KO libraries The Avana CRISPR gRNA library in HT29-Cas9 cells, containing four gRNAs targeting 18,675 annotated human protein-coding genes, was generated in two replicates (A and B) as previously described21. Libraries A and B were maintained at more than 500× representation in T225 flasks. Two independent screens, consisting of two rounds each of BFT selection, were performed on libraries A and B. One confluent T225 flask (around 120 million cells) of each library was treated with His6-tagged BFT (1.5 ng ml−1, 70 pM) in serum-free McCoy’s 5a medium for 1 h at 37 °C and 5% CO2. BFT-treated flasks were rinsed twice with Dulbecco’s PBS (DPBS) and treated with 12 ml of Cellstripper (Corning) for 40 min at 37 °C. Then, 15 ml of pre-warmed 2% FBS in DPBS was added and cells were gently dissociated by pipetting up and down. Cells were pelleted at 200g for 5 min, washed with 2% FBS/DPBS, pelleted again and resuspended in pre-warmed digestion solution (DPBS with 2% FBS, 100 μg ml−1 DNase I, 500 μg ml−1 collagenase D, 5 mM MgCl2 and 2 mM CaCl2) to further dissociate cell clumps. Cells were pelleted and washed with ice-cold FACS buffer (DPBS with 2% FBS and 2 mM CaCl2), and then resuspended in ice-cold FACS buffer with 1:100 PE-conjugated E-cadherin antibody and stained for 40 min at 4 °C with end-over-end rotation. Cells were sorted on an SH800S Cell Sorter (Sony) using a 70-μm nozzle and the top 10% of live, single cells by surface E-cadherin staining were collected. Collected cells were plated, expanded and subjected to the same procedure for the second round of selection. After each round of selection and expansion, genomic DNA was extracted from 10 million cells using the Blood and Cell Culture DNA Kit (Qiagen) and DNA fragments containing the gRNA sequences were amplified by PCR to attach Illumina adaptor and barcode sequences as previously described34 (Extended Data Fig. 2a). The same DNA extraction and PCR were performed on the unselected libraries A and B for comparison of gRNA abundances. PCR products were gel purified and sequenced on an Illumina MiSeq. Reads were trimmed to eliminate adaptor sequences using CLC Genomics Workbench (Qiagen) and the rank and statistical significance of genes after each round of selection was determined using MAGeCK22. The null distribution of the 1,000 Avana control gRNAs was used to compute P values for all genes using the MAGeCK ‘test’ function with the option ‘--norm-method control’. Hits were defined as genes significant at an FDR of 0.05 in round 2 of both screens, A and B. Full gene-level datasets for each screen replicate and round are available as Supplementary Tables 1–4.

BFT caecal injection assay All procedures were conducted in accordance with the guidelines approved by the Boston Children’s Hospital Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (no. 00002233). CD-1 outbred mice (5 weeks old, body weight around 17–20 g) were purchased from Envigo (030-US) and only the female mice were used. Mice were group housed with up to five animals per cage on a 12:12-h light:dark cycle, with free access to food and drink in individually ventilated specific-pathogen-free cages (temperature 22 ± 2 °C; relative humidity 40–60%). All mice used were healthy and were not involved in any previous procedures or drug treatments. For BFT caecal injection experiments, untagged BFT (10 μg), CLN4sol (300 μg) or C4sol(C2-ECS) (300 μg) was incubated either alone or mixed together in 200 μl of PBS for 30 min at room temperature. Mice were anaesthetized with isoflurane and the caecum was exposed via laparotomy. The BFT, CLNsol or BFT:CLNsol mixture was injected directly into the caecum, followed by wound closure with stitches. Buprenorphine (0.1 mg kg−1) was injected subcutaneously immediately after surgery for analgesia. Mice were allowed to recover, and 4 h after surgery, the mice were euthanized. The caecum was collected, rinsed with PBS to remove the contents and fixed with 10% formalin overnight for further histology and immunofluorescence analysis. The fixed caecum was dehydrated with 70% ethanol, 96% ethanol, 100% ethanol, then xylene (each step twice for 30 min), then infiltrated with melted paraffin at 58 °C for 45 min and embedded into the block. The tissue blocks were sectioned into 6-μm-thick sections. For H&E staining, sections were heated at 42 °C for 30 min and treated with xylene (twice for 5 min), 100% ethanol (thrice for 1 min), tap water (1 min), Gill 3 haematoxylin (2 min), tap water (2 min), eosin (3 min), 100% ethanol (thrice for 1 min) and xylene again (twice for 2 min). Sections were mounted with DPX mountant (Sigma) for histology analysis. Stained sections were coded and scored blindly. For immunofluorescence analysis, sections were heated at 42 °C for 30 min, then deparaffinized with xylene (twice for 10 min). The sections were air dried, then rehydrated with 100% ethanol, 70% ethanol, 50% ethanol, 30% ethanol, water and PBS (each step for 5 min). The rehydrated sections were immersed in slightly boiling 10 mM sodium citrate buffer pH 6.0 for 10 min, washed with PBS for 5 min, then incubated with blocking buffer (5% FBS, 0.1% Triton X-100 in PBS) for 1 h and with 1:100 rabbit anti-E-cadherin antibody overnight (3195T, Cell Signaling Technology). The next day, sections were washed three times with PBS and incubated with 1:100 DyLight488-conjugated donkey anti-rabbit IgG (406404, BioLegend) for 1 h at room temperature. Then the sections were washed three times with PBS and mounted with DAPI Fluoromount-G (SouthernBiotech). Images were recorded with an LSM880 upright confocal system (Zeiss) and processed in ImageJ. H&E-stained sections were scored in a blinded fashion for epithelial shedding and oedema (Supplementary Fig. 11). Measurement of caecal crypt length was performed as described in ref. 62. Specifically, ten

distinct crypts were randomly chosen from each section. Only crypts with an intact architecture spanning from the crypt base to the luminal surface were selected, and the selected crypts were distributed as evenly as possible across the entire caecal mucosa. Crypt length was measured using ImageJ. The average value of the ten measurements was used as the readout for each mouse.
